name: observable_unique_ptr / observer_ptr (oup)
workload: Median dereference/creation cost across int, float, std::string, std::array<int,65536> owned objects; oup::observer_ptr dereference vs std::weak_ptr::lock()-based dereference (also compares owner-pointer creation vs std::unique_ptr/shared_ptr)
claimed_speedup: Dereference observer/obs_unique and observer/obs_sealed measured at 1.0x relative to a raw-pointer baseline, vs 3.5x for weak/shared (i.e. observer_ptr dereference ~3.5x cheaper than std::weak_ptr::lock()-based dereference) on gcc 9.4.0/libstdc++-9/Ryzen 5 2600
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.4.0 (libstdc++-9) and MSVC 16.11.3; all optimizations turned on except LTO
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 2600, Linux 5.15.0 (gcc run); Intel i7-7800X, Windows 10.0.19043 (MSVC run)
tradeoffs: Not thread-safe (no atomic refcount), unlike std::shared_ptr/weak_ptr; no array support; no custom-allocator support; owner-pointer creation itself is 1.1-2.1x SLOWER than std::unique_ptr/shared_ptr in the same table, so the win is specific to the observer/dereference path.
caveats: The library is not a full shared_ptr replacement (unique-ownership only); the speed advantage shown is for dereferencing a non-owning observer pointer vs std::weak_ptr::lock(), not for construction/destruction, which is slower than std::unique_ptr.

name: CDRC atomic_weak_ptr (concurrent_deferred_rc)
baseline: just::thread's atomic<weak_ptr> (commercial third-party implementation of the C++20 std::atomic<std::weak_ptr> interface)
workload: Ramalethe & Correia lock-free concurrent doubly-linked queue using atomic weak back-pointers; P threads repeatedly pop-then-reinsert an element, P = 1 to 192, on a 4-socket 72-core machine
claimed_speedup: 67x faster than just::thread at P=1 thread; 4.2x faster at P=8 threads; ~10x faster at P=192 threads (own weak-pointer implementation is 19-33% slower than a hand-customized manual-memory-management baseline over the same range) (paper Fig. 12)
hardware: 4-socket 72-core machine, 4x Intel Xeon E7-8867 v4 @ 2.4GHz, 2-way hyperthreading, 45MB L3 cache, 1TB RAM
tradeoffs: Requires a C++20-concepts-capable compiler; full benchmark reproduction needs jemalloc + NUMA-aware setup; library is research-grade (from the CDRC/acquire-retire papers), not a drop-in std::shared_ptr replacement, and uses more memory than manual reclamation in oversubscribed scenarios.
caveats: The quoted numbers compare against just::thread, a commercial library implementing the std::atomic<weak_ptr> interface, not against libstdc++/libc++'s own atomic<weak_ptr> (which those stdlibs did not implement at the time); MSVC STL is the only mainstream stdlib with a native implementation and was not the one benchmarked here. Paper also reports a separate 2-3x throughput gain over prior concurrent-refcounting implementations (not vs std::shared_ptr directly).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "atomic_shared_ptr OR hazard pointer github lock-free faster than std::shared_ptr benchmark ns/op" -> paper citation in DanielLiamAnderson/atomic_shared_ptr README

name: Delegate (bdiamand/Delegate)
workload: Invocation-timing shootout (CxxFunctionBenchmark various.cpp) across function-pointer, compile-time-function-pointer, compile-time-delegate, non-assignable, lambda-capture and stateless-lambda call patterns, many iterations per category
claimed_speedup: Delegate consistently fastest of 13 implementations: 0.2101s vs std::function 0.2640s (function_pointer); 0.1324s vs 0.1884s (compile_time_function_pointer); 0.1396s vs 0.1906s (compile_time_delegate); 0.1402s vs 0.1860s (non_assignable); 0.1585s vs 0.1757s (lambda_capture); 0.1325s vs 0.1799s (stateless_lambda) (derived from page data, CxxFunctionBenchmark 'Sample Result')
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 64-bit, Visual Studio 15.9.4, Release build, Boost 1.69.0
tradeoffs: Fixed-size capture (8 bytes + capture size on 32-bit, +8 more on 64-bit); no arbitrary-size type erasure or allocator support like std::function; no LICENSE file included.
caveats: Numbers come from an independent third-party shootout (CxxFunctionBenchmark), not Delegate's own repo; CPU model is not stated in that shootout, capping the tier at B; repo itself has no benchmark of its own.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "github delegate.hpp entt faster than std::function no allocation benchmark"

name: stdext::inplace_function (WG21-SG14/SG14)
workload: Same CxxFunctionBenchmark various.cpp invocation-timing shootout as above
claimed_speedup: Faster than std::function in 5 of 7 categories: 0.2365s vs 0.2640s (function_pointer); 0.1583s vs 0.1884s (compile_time_function_pointer); 0.1593s vs 0.1906s (compile_time_delegate); 0.1855s vs 0.1897s (heavy_functor); 0.1589s vs 0.1860s (non_assignable); but slower in lambda_capture (0.1851s vs 0.1757s) and stateless_lambda (0.1845s vs 0.1799s) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Fixed-capacity buffer with no heap fallback: fails to compile/assign a callable that exceeds the configured capacity, unlike std::function which always works via heap allocation.
caveats: Mixed shootout results: loses to std::function specifically on stateless-lambda/lambda-capture cases where std::function's own small-object optimization already avoids heap allocation. inplace_function.h is one header inside the larger multi-proposal SG14 monorepo, not its own dedicated repo; the repo-level GitHub license field is empty, but the header itself carries a Boost Software License 1.0 notice. No CPU model stated in the shootout, capping tier at B.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "inplace_function github stack allocated std::function alternative benchmark"

name: SmallFunction (LoopPerfect/smallfunction)
workload: Construct+invoke 100 functors of varying stack-capture-buffer sizes (32-2048 bytes), stored in a vector and called in a loop, using Google Benchmark
claimed_speedup: README claims 3-5x faster than std::function; table shows e.g. sf64 369ns vs std::function 1141ns (g++6), sf64 310ns vs std::function 1511ns (clang++6/libc++) -- roughly 3.1-4.9x depending on buffer size/compiler
compiler_and_flags: g++6 and clang++6/libc++; optimization level not stated
tradeoffs: Stack capacity is a fixed compile-time template parameter (e.g. SmallFun<Sig,64>); no heap fallback for oversized captures, so it is not template-compatible drop-in replacement for arbitrary-size std::function usages.
caveats: First-party benchmark with a public numbers table but no stated optimization flags or CPU model, so capped at Tier C per rules even though the methodology is otherwise reasonable; project has had no commits since January 2018.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "inplace_function github stack allocated std::function alternative benchmark"
